html:
Lee Kuan Yew was the first prime minister of Singapore, from 1959 to 1990, and the main builder of the modern city-state. Under his rule a small colonial port became one of the richest countries in the world.

He was born in Singapore under British rule, to a family of Peranakan Chinese descent. The Japanese occupation of 1942 to 1945 convinced him that Britain could not protect the colony. He studied law at Cambridge, came home, and in 1954 co-founded the People's Action Party, which has governed Singapore ever since.

His path to power and independence:

  • He led the party to victory in 1959, when Singapore gained self-government.
  • He took Singapore into the new federation of Malaysia in 1963.
  • Racial and political quarrels with the federal government led to Singapore's expulsion in 1965. Lee wept on television announcing it.

Facing the new state's survival with no land, no water of its own and no army, his government:

  • Invited foreign companies to build factories, making Singapore one of the Four Asian Tigers.
  • Built public housing that now houses most of the population.
  • Made English the working language, while keeping Chinese, Malay and Tamil, and balanced its racial communities with strict rules.
  • Helped found ASEAN in 1967.

He governed with a hard hand: detention without trial, lawsuits against critics, and a tightly controlled press. Leaders from Deng Xiaoping onward studied his model of growth without liberal democracy. After stepping down he stayed in cabinet until 2011, and his son became prime minister in 2004. He traced the city's modern story back to the British founding of 1819.
